newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian family beheaded, four others slain on bus.
newsitem.headline: Colombian family beheaded, four others slain on bus.

text.p: A family of eight was beheaded by a right-wing paramilitary gang and unidentified killers gunned down four people on a bus in two separate attacks in northwest Colombia, police said on Saturday.

The first attack took place on Friday afternoon in the village of Tascon, in Antioquia province. Police said a heavily-armed paramilitary gang broke into the peasant family's house and decapitated them with machetes. They then hacked the bodies to pieces and dumped the remains of five of the victims into the nearby Riosucio River.

Official reports on the incident were still sketchy on Saturday because of the remote location of the village -- at the gateway to the violence-torn, banana-growing region of Uraba, traditionally the scene of some of the heaviest battles between paramilitaries, leftist guerrillas and the army.
Police could not say how many women and children had died in the massacre because only three corpses were found in the house. The other bodies had not been recovered from the river.
Tascon is near the town of Dabeiba, where Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) rebels have partially blocked the main highway between Medellin and Uraba for two weeks.
Counterinsurgency operations and aerial bombardments by the air force have so far failed to shift the rebels from the mountainous, jungle-covered region.
The second attack took place on Saturday morning in Medellin, Colombia's third largest city, also in Antioquia.

A police spokesman said an undetermined number of gunmen with automatic weapons boarded a bus and sprayed bullets into three men and a 15-year-old boy. Autopsies showed each body was shot between 10 and 20 times, the Medellin police spokesman said.

He said the motive for the attack and the killers' identities were being investigated, adding that two of the dead were former Marxist guerrillas who had laid down their arms and returned to civilian life.
Rebels who abandon the armed struggle are often targeted by former comrades who regard them as deserters and by paramilitaries who see them as potential subversives.
